newsitem.title: UK: UK may buy out or tax lottery consortium-minister.
newsitem.headline: UK may buy out or tax lottery consortium-minister.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government, angered by steep salary rises for national lottery executives, may consider buying out the consortium or slapping a windfall tax on it.
But National Heritage Secretary Chris Smith warned on Thursday that the contract would be difficult to change and a buyout could be expensive.
Prime Minister Tony Blair was outraged by reports that the executive salary bill at lottery operator Camelot Group Plc had risen by 40 percent while the sums it raised for good causes had fallen.

Camelot, owned by a consortium of five British and foreign companies, said the total raised for good causes such as charities, sports and the arts dropped to 1.27 billion pounds in the year to March from 1.42 billion pounds 12 months earlier.
Heritage Secretary Smith summoned Camelot chief executive Tim Holley to an urgent meeting after his pay package was increased by 53 percent to 590,000 pounds.
"I am going to say very clearly the very key message that the national lottery is for prizewinners and the good causes. It is not for profiteering. I am very angry indeed," he told BBC Radio.
Labour, which won a landslide election victory on May 1, wants the lottery handed over to a non-profit organisation when Camelot's licence expires in 2001.
Asked if the government might consider buying out Camelot or slapping a windfall tax on its profits, Smith said: "We will need to consider that as a possible option. But it is probably expensive.
"They have a legal contract entered into by the previous government. It may be very difficult to change."
Smith said: "The cost of buying it out might be excessive to the public purse. We will of course look at all options."

Asked about the chances of Camelot winning the lottery contract again after 2001, he said: "If they want to have any hope of doing that, then they have to make sure they are acting with public approval and probity now.
"Unfortunately they are operating under a contract. They are legally entitled to do this. This is part of the mess we have inherited," Smith said.
"It is precisely why we want to go for a not-for-profit lottery in the near future and we are bringing forward legislation later this year to do so," he said.
The lottery, launched in November 1994, attracts 30 million Britons every week who are attracted by get-rich jackpots that can top 10 million pounds.

But critics have slammed the hugely popular lottery and churchmen say it encourages gambling. The tabloid media launched a full-scale assault on Thursday, accusing the Camelot executives of being "greedy fat cats."
Camelot is owned by Cadbury Schweppes PLC, De La Rue Plc, GTECH UK, Racal Electronics and ICL.
